question.text:
The index node (inode) of a Unix-like file system contains $\mathbf{10}$ direct pointers, one singleindirect pointer, and one triple-indirect pointer. The disk block size is $\mathbf{8 ~kB}$, and each disk block address is $\mathbf{64-}$bits long.

The maximum possible file size is (rounded off to $\mathbf{2}$ decimal places) $\_\_\_\_  ~\mathbf{TB}$.

question.text:
Consider the following set of processes to be scheduled on a single CPU using the Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) algorithm.

\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\text{Process} & \text{Arrival (ms)} & \text{Execution (ms)}\\
P1 & 0 & 8\\
P2 & 2 & 4\\
P3 & 4 & 2\\
P4 & 5 & 1\\
P5 & 8 & 3
\end{array}
\]
 

The average process turnaround time (in msec) is $\_\_\_\_$ .

question.text:
In a multi-processing operating system, deadlock prevention is implemented using a prioritybased timestamping scheme. Every process is assigned a unique timestamp when it enters the system. If a process is killed and restarted, it retains its original timestamp.

Let $P_{\text {req }}$ be a process requesting a resource $R$, and $P_{\text {hold }}$ be the process currently holding resource $R$. Let $T\left(P_{r c q}\right)$ and $T\left(P_{\text {hold }}\right)$ represent their respective timestamps (where a smaller timestamp indicates an older process).

The system uses the following algorithm to decide whether a process should wait or be killed:

if T(Preq) > T(Phold) then
    kill Preq
else
    wait
  1. THE SCHEME IS DEADLOCK-FREE, BUT NOT STARVATION-FREE
     
  2. THE SCHEME IS NOT DEADLOCK-FREE, BUT STARVATION-FREE
     
  3. THE SCHEME IS NEITHER DEADLOCK-FREE NOR STARVATION-FREE
     
  4. THE SCHEME IS BOTH DEADLOCK-FREE AND STARVATION-FREE
question.subject: Operating System

question.text:
In a system, there are three types of resources$: \mathbf{R1}$, $\mathbf{R2}$, and $\mathbf{R3}$. Four processes $\mathbf{P0}$, $\mathbf{P1}$, $\mathbf{P2}$, and $\mathbf{P3}$ execute concurrently. The processes have declared their maximum resource requirements and their current allocations as shown in the tables below.

Consider a state of the system where the currently available resources are: Available$\mathbf{: [R1: 2, R2: 1, R3: 0]}$
 

Resource Matrices

\begin{array}{ccc}
\text { Process } & \text { Allocation (R1 R2 R3) } & \text { Max (R1 R2 R3) } \\
\textbf{ P0 } & 0~1~0 & 7~5~3 \\
\textbf { P1 } & 2~0~0 & 3~2~2 \\
\textbf { P2 } & 3~0~2 & 9~0~2 \\
\textbf { P3 } & 2~1~1 & 2~2~2
\end{array}

From the perspective of deadlock avoidance, which one of the following is true?

  1. THE SYSTEM IS IN A SAFE STATE
     
  2. THE SYSTEM IS NOT IN A SAFE STATE, BUT WOULD BE SAFE IF ONE MORE INSTANCE OF $\mathrm{R1}$ WERE AVAILABLE
     
  3. THE SYSTEM IS NOT IN A SAFE STATE, BUT WOULD BE SAFE IF ONE MORE INSTANCE OF $\mathrm{R3}$ WERE AVAILABLE
     
  4. THE SYSTEM IS NOT IN A SAFE STATE, BUT WOULD BE SAFE IF TWO MORE INSTANCE OF $\mathrm{R2}$ AND ONE INSTANCE OF $\mathrm{R3}$ WERE AVAILABLE
question.subject: Operating System

question.text:
Consider a uniprogrammed operating system where only one user process executes at a time, and the process performs disk I/O requests sequentially. The disk scheduling policy initially used is SCAN.

Suppose the disk scheduling algorithm is replaced with Shortest Seek Time First (SSTF), and the system vendor claims that this change results in a $\mathbf{40 \%}$ reduction in average disk head movement during benchmarking.

What is the expected improvement in the overall I/O performance perceived by the user process?

  1. $40 \%$
     
  2. $20 \%$
     
  3. $0\%$
     
  4. Depends on the disk queue length
question.subject: Operating System
